BREAKING: The Texas midterm numbers are raising eyebrows all across America because they simply do not add up. Now, Will Caiin of Fox News is sounding the alarm like nobody else ever has.

When you break down the very specific numbers, it's easy to see that something is afoot.

"Republicans get 4.5 million votes, again, same as they did for the last 3 midterms or so," Cain said on his latest podcast episode. 

"Democrats jump from where they'd been consistently at 3.5 to 5.2. 1.7 million new votes for Democrats."

That's a jump of nearly 50 percent. In one cycle.

So where did 1.7 million new Democratic votes come from? The analyst ran through the explanations, and none of them work.

Population growth? 

"Only 1.4 million people have moved to Texas over the last 4 years. That's bigger than that," Cain continued.

"If you say Rs voted Ds, well, then why did the Rs stay in stasis and the Ds jumped?"

"This needs to be understood. Even if all in the end your understanding is, how did Democrats mobilize... How did they do that? That's wild," Cain concluded.

So the question everyone should be asking...where did 1.7 million votes come from?

Visiting Auschwitz and Birkenau was a harrowing experience.

My wife Yasmine and I viewed the possessions left behind by the victims and visited the barracks, gas chambers, and crematoria. Every shoe and suitcase was a reminder of a human being who had a name, a family and a life.

The crimes of the Holocaust against the Jewish people are incomparable in the combination of its industrial scale of slaughter and the bureaucratic efficiency with which it was planned and organized. Auschwitz and Birkenau lay that plain.

My thoughts turned to the people of Iran, and to a regime that denies the Holocaust while attempting to erase the massacre of our compatriots from the world’s memory through internet blackouts, censorship and hidden executions.

But the Islamic Republic does not represent Iran. The heirs of Cyrus stand with the Jewish people. And while the regime seeks death and destruction, the Iranian nation is fighting for life and liberty.

We placed a wreath bearing the Lion and Sun on behalf of the Iranian people at the memorial to the victims. We will never forget and we will not allow the regime occupying Iran to turn our nation’s name and history into instruments of hatred.

A free Iran will once again stand for peace, life and human dignity.

Light will prevail over darkness.

@AuschwitzMuseum @EJAssociation

posts.text:
🇷🇺 Moscow floats non-aggression pacts with individual NATO members, as Medinsky says Europe's security order was the real topic in Abu Dhabi

Russia has started to put its own vision for Europe's security on paper, and it works country by country.

Alexey Drobinin, head of foreign policy planning at the Russian Foreign Ministry, told a security forum on Wednesday that Moscow sees three models. The first is a defensive alliance or bilateral mutual assistance treaties, like those Russia has with Belarus and North Korea. The second is a political pledge not to help each other's adversaries in case of aggression, like Moscow's pact with Iran. The third is bilateral non-aggression pacts.

"For example, agreements of this kind could be reached, among other things, with individual NATO member states, which would then receive, for instance, additional individual security guarantees from the Russian Federation," Drobinin said, according to video of the speech reported by Reuters. TASS quoted him as framing it under the principle of "equal and indivisible security," the same language Moscow used in its December 2021 treaty drafts before the full-scale invasion.

The timing is deliberate. Vladimir Medinsky said a new security framework for Europe had been the central theme of the two days of talks in Abu Dhabi, according to Reuters, though he gave no details. US officials have said they are open to discussing Europe's overall security architecture. Some European politicians reject that, arguing a ceasefire in Ukraine must come first.

The appeal for Moscow is obvious. Separate deals with individual allies would offer each capital a private Russian guarantee and quietly weaken NATO's collective commitment under Article 5. No NATO government had publicly responded in the reports reviewed, and Drobinin's remarks are a proposal from a Foreign Ministry official, not an offer tabled in the talks as far as is known.

For the US, the question is how far the Abu Dhabi track drifts into redesigning European security while Washington is also floating an "Article 5-like" guarantee for Ukraine. For Europeans, it is whether they can shape that conversation before others do it for them.

What to watch: whether Kushner and Witkoff hear the same menu from Putin in Moscow on Thursday, and how NATO capitals respond in Dublin.

Joint NATO Defence of the Baltic Sea Post-Nuclear First Strike (Hypothetical).

Strategic Context.

In this hypothetical conflict, following intelligence preparation of the battlefield by drone reconnaissance, Russia initiates a limited tactical nuclear first strike targeting key NATO military installations in the Baltic region, including airfields in Denmark, Sweden, Poland, and the Baltics. The strikes—delivered by Iskander-M missiles or air-launched from Tu-22M bombers—aim to decapitate NATO’s airpower by cratering runways, destroying hangars, and contaminating sites with radiation. This disrupts conventional operations, causing immediate casualties, electromagnetic pulse (EMP) effects on electronics, and logistical chaos, while escalating the conflict toward potential strategic nuclear exchange. NATO’s response invokes Article 5, mobilizing a joint Nordic-Baltic defence.

Russia follows with a conventional air superiority push from Kaliningrad and the Baltic Fleet, deploying Su-35S fighters alongside Su-30SMs, Su-34s, and MiG-31 interceptors to seize control over the Baltic Sea, targeting shipping lanes, Gotland Island, and NATO resupply routes. The objective: Prevent NATO reinforcements from the North Sea and establish a no-fly zone, exploiting the nuclear shock to demoralize allies.

Denmark’s Royal Danish Air Force and Sweden’s Swedish Air Force lead the aerial defence. They integrate F-35As (Danish) and Gripen Es (Swedish) in a networked “Nordic Air Tasking Order.” Support includes Finnish F/A-18s, Polish F-16s, and NATO AWACS for shared battlespace awareness.

Nuclear First Strikes Severely Disrupt Fixed-base Operations.

Airfield Damage: Craters render runways unusable for days to weeks without rapid repair teams; fuel depots and ammo bunkers ignite, grounding ~50% of aircraft initially. Radiation fallout limits personnel exposure, reducing sortie rates.

NATO Adaptation: Gripen E’s dispersed basing doctrine shines—Sweden scrambles from highways and forest clearings, launching in under 10 minutes with minimal support. Danish F-35As, more airfield-dependent, relocate to hardened shelters or covert forward-operating bases in Norway/Finland. Overall, NATO air sortie generation drops 50–70% in the first 24 hours but recovers via redundancy.

Russian Gains/Losses: Kaliningrad’s airbase avoids direct hits but faces retaliatory conventional strikes; Russian aircraft suffer from EMP-disrupted comms, reducing coordination.

Joint NATO Defensive Tactics.

Under NATO’s Air Command, Danish F-35As act as “quarterbacks,” using stealth and sensor fusion to cue Gripen Es via datalinks for “loyal wingman” strikes.

Critical Phases.

Early Warning and BVR Phase (~100–200 km): Integrated radars and AWACS detect Russian incursions early. F-35As ambush Su-35s, firing AIM-120D AMRAAMs. Gripens follow with MBDA Meteors, achieving 70–80% hit rates. Joint Nordic patrols create overlapping coverage over Gotland and Bornholm.

WVR and Close Air Superiority Phase (<50 km): If Russians penetrate, Gripens’ agility handles dogfights, while F-35s provide offboard targeting. IRIS-T (Gripen) and AIM-9X (F-35) missiles counter R-73/R-77 threats. EW suites jam Russian Irbis-E radars.

Sustained Capabilities.

Sustained NATO Operations: Gripen’s low cost enables high sortie rates from dispersed sites; F-35’s fusion integrates with ground-based SAMs for layered defence.

Russian Offensive Capabilities: Su-35S supported by Su-30SMs for suppression of enemy air defences and MiG-31s for long-range intercepts. Armed with R-37M missiles, they aim for high-speed sweeps to clear NATO combat air patrols. Post-strike, Russians exploit chaos with low-level ingress to evade radars, using IRST to target stealthy F-35s.

Our message to Nvidia's board:

Do not fire Jensen Huang.

There is no clear replacement for Jensen Huang. We are confident that his departure would ultimately be a net negative for Nvidia, its shareholders, and the AI Revolution.

First, take a look at the data. History also suggests that removing a successful CEO will come with a significant cost.

A study of 187 forced CEO departures from S&P 1500 companies found that removing outperforming CEOs resulted in negative long-term stock returns. This case would be no different, in our view.

Jensen Huang is the definition of an outperforming CEO. Nvidia's board must not make a decision in the heat of the moment.

The board should take the time to conduct a thorough investigation and consult with shareholders, with a strong emphasis on the latter.

Quite literally, Nvidia's board should convene a special shareholder meeting and hold an advisory vote on this decision. This is the most consequential CEO controversy in world history. Shareholders deserve a say.

In addition, Nvidia's stock, $NVDA, is now down -35% in 26 trading days, nearly half of which is a result of the recent scandal.

We believe Jensen Huang's potential removal as CEO is now ~80% priced in.

Why take an action with massive downside potential when the market has already priced in much of that risk?

The downside of retaining Huang may be limited, while the potential upside is tremendous.

Lastly, history shows that retaining Jensen Huang could still lead to a favorable outcome. In 2019, Amazon retained Jeff Bezos as CEO after his extramarital affair became public, and the company's stock subsequently surged +108% by 2021.

Personal misconduct should not be ignored, but it must also be distinguished from corporate wrongdoing and weighed against the consequences of removing an executive who is instrumental to the company's success.

We believe Jensen Huang is an irreplaceable part of Nvidia and the AI Revolution more broadly.

Once the dust settles, firing Jensen Huang would prove to be a costly mistake.

It is time to pause and consult your shareholders.

Korean media report that LG Chem has begun developing materials for mass reflow molded underfill (MR-MUF), a key process in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) manufacturing. The company has reportedly made significant technical progress in developing non-conductive film (NCF), with promising results in recent evaluations, and is now expanding its work to include MR-MUF materials.

Samsung Electronics currently sources most of its NCF from Japan’s Resonac, while SK hynix sources its MR-MUF materials from another Japanese supplier, Namics. According to the reports, if LG Chem’s development efforts succeed, HBM manufacturers such as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix could reduce their reliance on Japanese materials and diversify their supply chains.
